summary:
Mission Forge is a browser game in which players build and launch a small orbiter into space on the moon. They select their bus, solar array, battery, radio, thruster, instruments and orbit and launcher. Health meters are trade-offs and live success probability will indicate the risk prior to launch. Then the mission unfolds through events and decisions that include a solar storm which necessitates a choice between safe mode and continued science. Players earn a score, stars and achievements. Errors are described in simple terms with their own numbers, and the errors are followed by a retrial loop for them to correct the design.
The rocket equation, the power and eclipse budgets, the radio link budget and a Monte Carlo simulation of 1000 uncertain flights; battery uncertainty derived from NASA test data all behind the game is real engineering. Each number is accompanied by a provenance badge indicating whether it is measured, published, calculated or illustrative.
It is important because it is the way mission design and uncertainty can be understood, it demonstrates that spaceflight is not about luck, but about margins, trade-offs and honest assumptions.
details:
What it does:

Mission Forge turns spacecraft engineering trade offs into a game. The player picks an orbit, a launch vehicle, parts and instruments for a lunar mission, with live mass, power, budget and data limits. A pre-launch check explains every warning and locks options that cannot work. The mission then flies with events and decisions, followed by a Reality Check that reruns the design 1,000 times with uncertain parameters. The final report gives a score, stars, achievements, a comparison with real lunar orbiters (Lunar Reconnaissance Orbiter, Lunar Prospector and KPLO), and, if the mission failed, a plain-words reason with a suggested fix and a retry.

Benefits and impact:

Students rarely get to see how mission decisions affect each other. Here a bigger instrument costs mass and power, a bigger battery costs mass and money, and a design that passes on paper can still fail under uncertainty. Failures are never "bad luck": each one names the cause using the player's own numbers.

Data:

We used the NASA PCoE battery data set to set the spread of battery wear in the Reality Check, the NASA Moon Fact Sheet for orbit calculations, and the NASA LRO/LCROSS press kit for real mission figures. Every number is labelled Measured (analogue), Published, Calculated or Illustrative. The battery spread comes from only four lab cells, and the average wear and the event effects are game assumptions. The result is simulated reliability under stated assumptions, not a real flight probability.

Tools:

HTML, CSS and JavaScript (ES modules only), Python with NumPy and SciPy for the offline battery analysis, Visual Studio Code, GitHub for the code, and Render for hosting.

Creativity:

We combined a real engineering model with a game loop of build, launch, decide, learn and retry, and made the Reality Check the memorable moment of the game.

AI assistance:

We used Claude for brainstorming.

Link: https://missionforge-4mdk.onrender.com/

GitHub: https://github.com/Koishna/MissionForge
